questions.text:
Consider the following read-write schedule [latex] S [/latex] over three transactions [latex] T_1, T_2 [/latex], and [latex] T_3 [/latex], where the subscripts in the schedule indicate transaction IDs:

[latex] S: r_1(z) ; w_1(z) ; r_2(x) ; r_3(y) ; w_3(y) ; r_2(y) ; w_2(x) ; w_2(y) ; [/latex]

Which of the following transaction schedules is/are conflict equivalent to [latex] S [/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write):
- z: only T1 uses it [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1 has no conflict with anyone.
- x: only T2 uses it.
- y: [latex]r_3(y),w_3(y)[/latex] come before [latex]r_2(y),w_2(y)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3 must come before T2.

So any serial order with T3 before T2 is conflict equivalent, and T1 can be anywhere: [latex]T_1T_3T_2,\;T_3T_2T_1,\;T_3T_1T_2[/latex].
[latex]T_1T_2T_3[/latex] puts T2 before T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not equivalent.

Answer: [latex]T_1T_3T_2[/latex], [latex]T_3T_2T_1[/latex], [latex]T_3T_1T_2[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider a Boolean expression given by [latex] F(X, Y, Z)=\Sigma(3,5,6,7) [/latex].
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Minterms 3, 5, 6, 7 = 011, 101, 110, 111 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] F = 1 when at least two inputs are 1 (majority function).

- Maxterms are the remaining combinations: [latex]\Pi(0,1,2,4)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Majority function [latex]=XY+YZ+XZ[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Depends on Y: [latex]F(1,0,0)=0[/latex] but [latex]F(1,1,0)=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] so not independent of Y.
- Depends on X: [latex]F(0,1,0)=0[/latex] but [latex]F(1,1,0)=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] so not independent of X.

Answer: [latex]F=\Pi(0,1,2,4)[/latex] and [latex]F=XY+YZ+XZ[/latex]

Each iteration does [latex]x\leftarrow2x+y[/latex], repeated [latex]y[/latex] times. Solving:
[latex]f(x,y)=2^y x+(2^y-1)y=2^y(x+y)-y[/latex]

- [latex]x=20,y=10[/latex]: [latex]1024\times30-10=30710[/latex]. This is less than [latex]2^{20}[/latex] but more than [latex]2^{10}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] options 1 and 3 FALSE.
- [latex]x=20,y=20[/latex]: [latex]2^{20}\times40-20 \gt 2^{20}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]x=10,y=20[/latex]: [latex]2^{20}\times30-20 \gt 2^{20}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] TRUE.
(Both values are about [latex]4\times10^7[/latex], so no int overflow.)

Answer: Options 2 and 4

questions.text: Let [latex] A [/latex] be any [latex] n \times m [/latex] matrix, where [latex] m > n [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the system of linear equations [latex] A x=0 [/latex] ?
questions.solution:
[latex]rank(A)\le n \lt m[/latex], so the solution space has dimension [latex]m-rank(A)\ge m-n[/latex].

- At least [latex]m-n[/latex] linearly independent solutions [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "[latex]m-n[/latex] vectors span every solution" fails when the dimension is larger, e.g. A = zero matrix (dimension m) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=[1\;\;1][/latex] ([latex]n=1,m=2[/latex]): solutions are [latex]t(1,-1)[/latex]; no non-zero solution has a zero entry, though [latex]m-n=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex]: solutions [latex](0,0,t)[/latex] have only 1 non-zero variable [latex]\lt n=2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: There exist at least [latex]m-n[/latex] linearly independent solutions

options: There exist at least [latex] m-n [/latex] linearly independent solutions to this system
There exist [latex] m-n [/latex] linearly independent vectors such that every solution is a linear combination of these vectors
There exists a non-zero solution in which at least [latex] m-n [/latex] variables are 0
There exists a solution in which at least [latex] n [/latex] variables are non-zero

questions.text:
Consider the 5 -state DFA [latex] M [/latex] accepting the language [latex] L(M) \subset(0+1)^* [/latex] shown below. For any string [latex] w \in(0+1)^* [/latex] let [latex] n_0(w) [/latex] be the number of [latex] 0^{\prime} s [/latex] in [latex] w [/latex] and [latex] n_1(w) [/latex] be the number of 1 's in [latex] w [/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.solution:
Reading 0 moves 1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]3[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1, reading 1 moves 1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]4[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]5[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1, and the reverse arrows undo a step. So the DFA tracks [latex](n_0-n_1)\bmod 3[/latex]:
state 1 = 0, states 2 and 5 = 1, states 3 and 4 = 2.

[latex]L(M)=\{w: n_0(w)\equiv n_1(w)\pmod 3\}[/latex], and states with the same value are equivalent.

- 2 and 4 (values 1 and 2): distinguishable (input "1": 2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1 accept, 4[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]5 reject) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- 3 and 4: both value 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] equivalent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] statement FALSE.
- 2 and 5: both value 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] equivalent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] statement FALSE.
- [latex]n_0=n_1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] difference 0 [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] accepted [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: "States 3 and 4 are distinguishable" and "States 2 and 5 are distinguishable"

States 3 and 4 are distinguishable in [latex] M [/latex]
States 2 and 5 are distinguishable in [latex] M [/latex]
Any string [latex] w [/latex] with [latex] n_0(w)=n_1(w) [/latex] is in [latex] L(M) [/latex]
